txn:36620.description: Hesperornis was a large, cormorant-like toothed seabird from the Late Cretaceous. Virtually wingless, it swam with powerful hind legs, diving for fish in the shallow seas that then covered North America. Like some other Mesozoic birds it kept teeth, set in a groove along the jaw.

notableFacts.text: Virtually wingless — it swam with powerful hind legs and could barely move on land.
Kept teeth set in a groove along the jaw, unlike modern birds.
A specialised foot-propelled diver of the Cretaceous seaways.

txn:36620.oneLiner: A large, flightless, toothed diving bird of the Cretaceous seas.

txn:38511.description: Herrerasaurus was a lightly built carnivorous dinosaur of the Late Triassic of Argentina, about 6 m long, and one of the earliest dinosaurs known. Its fragmentary early finds long made its classification uncertain until a near-complete skeleton was found.

notableFacts.text: Among the earliest known dinosaurs.
Named after Victorino Herrera, the rancher who found the first specimen.

txn:38511.oneLiner: One of the earliest dinosaurs, a Late Triassic predator.

txn:38520.description: Coelophysis was a small, slenderly built, bipedal carnivore from the Late Triassic of the southwestern United States, up to about 3 m long. One of the earliest known dinosaur genera, it is among the most specimen-rich — famous mass-death assemblages at Ghost Ranch preserve hundreds of individuals.

notableFacts.text: One of the earliest known dinosaurs.
Known from hundreds of individuals, including the famous Ghost Ranch death assemblages.

txn:38520.oneLiner: A small, slender, early carnivorous dinosaur of the Late Triassic.

txn:38522.description: Dilophosaurus was a theropod predator of Early Jurassic North America, about 7 m long, named for the pair of thin crests on its skull. It was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs.

notableFacts.text: Named for the pair of thin, arching crests on its skull.
Portrayed with a frill and venom in Jurassic Park — both fictional.

txn:38522.oneLiner: An Early Jurassic predator with a pair of head crests.

txn:38528.description: Coelurus was a small, lightly built bipedal carnivore of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming, with elongate legs and hollow tail bones. Though it gave its name to the Coelurosauria, it has long been poorly understood.
txn:38528.nameMeaning: "Hollow tail", for its hollow tail vertebrae

notableFacts.text: Gave its name to the Coelurosauria, though it remains poorly known.
A small, slender, long-legged predator.

txn:38528.oneLiner: A small, lightly built theropod of the Morrison Formation.

txn:38538.description: Compsognathus was a small, bipedal carnivore about the size of a chicken from the Late Jurassic of Europe. It is one of the few dinosaurs whose diet is known for certain — the remains of small, agile lizards are preserved in the bellies of both known specimens. It was long the smallest known non-avian dinosaur.

notableFacts.text: About the size of a chicken — long the smallest known non-avian dinosaur.
Its last meals — small lizards — are preserved in its stomach.

txn:38538.oneLiner: A tiny, chicken-sized carnivorous theropod of the Late Jurassic.

txn:38544.description: Ornithomimus was a swift, feathered ornithomimid of Late Cretaceous western North America, with long legs and a small toothless beak that hints at an omnivorous diet. It is one of the classic 'ostrich dinosaurs'.

notableFacts.text: Some specimens preserve evidence of feathers, including wing-like arm plumage.
Its toothless beak suggests an omnivorous diet.

txn:38545.description: Struthiomimus was an ornithomimid ('ostrich dinosaur') of Late Cretaceous western North America — a long-legged, bipedal, toothless-beaked runner. Its abundance and beak suggest it was an opportunistic omnivore.

notableFacts.text: Long-legged and ostrich-like, built for running.
Its toothless beak suggests an opportunistic, largely plant-based omnivorous diet.

txn:38547.description: Gallimimus was the largest known ornithomimid ('ostrich dinosaur'), from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia — about 6 m long with long legs, a small head, large side-facing eyes and a toothless horny beak. Like its relatives it was likely feathered and built for speed.

notableFacts.text: The largest known ornithomimid ('ostrich dinosaur').
Toothless, with a horny beak; likely feathered and fast-running.
Had large, side-facing eyes on a small, light head.

txn:38547.oneLiner: The largest 'ostrich dinosaur', a long-legged, toothless runner.

txn:38553.description: Therizinosaurus was a colossal therizinosaurid of Late Cretaceous Mongolia, 9–10 m long and up to 5 m tall, famous for its gigantic scythe-like hand claws. Despite being a theropod, it was a slow, long-necked, high-browsing herbivore with a horny beak and a wide gut.

notableFacts.text: Its scythe-like hand claws were among the largest of any known animal.
A theropod that became a slow-moving, long-necked herbivore.

txn:38559.description: Oviraptor was a small, feathered oviraptorid from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, 1.6–2 m long, with a toothless beak and probably a head crest. It was named 'egg thief' because its first skeleton was found atop a nest of eggs — later shown to be its own nest, which it was brooding, not raiding.

notableFacts.text: 'Egg thief' is a misnomer — the eggs it was found with were its own.
Later oviraptorid finds show these dinosaurs brooded their nests like birds.
Had a toothless beak and probably a head crest.

txn:38559.oneLiner: A small feathered oviraptorid, famously misjudged as an egg-thief.

txn:38562.description: Deinonychus was a dromaeosaurid theropod up to about 3.4 m long from the Cretaceous of North America, bearing an enlarged, sickle-shaped killing claw on each foot. John Ostrom's study of it in the 1960s revolutionised views of dinosaurs as active, agile, possibly warm-blooded animals — igniting the 'dinosaur renaissance'.
txn:38562.nameMeaning: "Terrible claw", for the sickle claw on its foot

notableFacts.text: Its enlarged sickle-shaped foot claw gives it its name, 'terrible claw'.
Ostrom's 1960s study of it sparked the 'dinosaur renaissance'.
The real-life basis for the 'raptors' of Jurassic Park, which used the name Velociraptor.

txn:38562.oneLiner: The sickle-clawed raptor that sparked the 'dinosaur renaissance'.

txn:38564.description: Velociraptor was a small bipedal, feathered carnivore with a long tail and an enlarged sickle-shaped claw on each hindfoot used to tackle and restrain prey. It lived in Late Cretaceous Asia (Mongolia and China) and is distinguished by its long, low, upturned snout. Roughly the size of a turkey, it was far smaller than its Jurassic Park portrayal, which was based on the larger Deinonychus.

notableFacts.text: Had an enlarged sickle-shaped claw on each hindfoot to restrain prey.
Was a feathered dinosaur.
A famous specimen preserves a Velociraptor locked in combat with a Protoceratops.
Only about the size of a turkey — much smaller than in film.

txn:38564.oneLiner: A small, feathered, sickle-clawed dromaeosaurid predator.

txn:38567.description: Saurornitholestes was a small, bipedal, meat-eating dromaeosaurid from the Late Cretaceous of Canada and the United States, equipped with a sickle-shaped claw on each foot. It is one of the more common small theropods of the Dinosaur Park Formation.

notableFacts.text: Bore a sickle-shaped killing claw on each foot.
First specimen found by amateur paleontologist Irene Vanderloh in 1974.

txn:38567.oneLiner: A small, sickle-clawed dromaeosaur of Late Cretaceous North America.

txn:38572.description: Troodon is a small, bird-like theropod from the Late Cretaceous of North America, named for its serrated 'wounding' teeth. Those teeth actually resemble those of herbivorous reptiles, hinting at a possibly omnivorous diet. Its taxonomy is controversial — the genus is based on a single tooth.

notableFacts.text: Named for its serrated 'wounding' teeth.
Its tooth shape hints at a possibly omnivorous diet.
Controversial — the genus rests on a single tooth.

txn:38572.oneLiner: A small, bird-like theropod named for its distinctive serrated teeth.

txn:38582.description: Majungasaurus was an abelisaurid theropod of latest-Cretaceous Madagascar, about 7 m long, with a short, deep snout, tiny arms, and a single rounded horn on top of its skull. It was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs, and bite-marked bones show it practised cannibalism.

notableFacts.text: Had a single rounded horn on the roof of its skull.
Bite-marked bones show it fed on others of its own kind.

txn:38582.oneLiner: A short-snouted, single-horned predator of Cretaceous Madagascar.

txn:38583.description: Megalosaurus was a large carnivorous theropod from the Middle Jurassic of southern England. Named by William Buckland in 1824, it was the first dinosaur genus to be validly named. Because no complete skeleton has been found, much about its build is still unclear; early naturalists even mistook it for a giant quadrupedal lizard.

notableFacts.text: The first dinosaur genus to be validly named (Buckland, 1824).
One of the three genera Richard Owen used to define Dinosauria in 1842.
Inspired one of the famous Crystal Palace dinosaur sculptures.

txn:38583.oneLiner: A Middle Jurassic theropod — the first dinosaur ever scientifically named.

txn:38590.description: Allosaurus was a large bipedal predator with a light but robust skull bearing dozens of sharp, serrated teeth, small three-fingered hands, and a long muscular tail. It averaged about 8.5 m long, with the largest specimens near 9.7 m. As the most abundant large predator of the Morrison Formation, it was the apex predator, likely hunting ornithopods, stegosaurids and sauropods.
txn:38590.nameMeaning: "Different lizard", for its unusually lightweight vertebrae

notableFacts.text: Its light skull bore dozens of sharp, serrated teeth.
The most abundant large predator of the Morrison Formation.
Whether it hunted in packs or was solitary remains debated.

txn:38590.oneLiner: The apex predatory theropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation.

txn:38598.description: Spinosaurus was among the largest known terrestrial carnivores, with a long, low, narrow crocodile-like skull bearing straight conical teeth, robust clawed forelimbs, short legs, and a paddle-like tail. Its trademark neural spines, over 1.65 m long, likely supported a skin sail. It lived in Cretaceous North Africa and ate both aquatic and terrestrial prey.

notableFacts.text: Its tall neural spines (over 1.65 m) likely supported a skin sail.
Ate both aquatic and terrestrial prey, with a crocodile-like snout.
The original 1912 remains were destroyed in World War II; new material emerged in the 21st century.

txn:38598.oneLiner: A giant sail-backed, semiaquatic fish-eating theropod.

txn:38600.description: Ceratosaurus was a carnivorous theropod of the Late Jurassic of North America and Europe, distinguished by a prominent horn on its snout and small hornlets over its eyes. It shared the Morrison Formation with the larger predator Allosaurus.

notableFacts.text: Bore a distinctive blade-like horn on its snout.
Had a row of small bony osteoderms down its back.

txn:38600.oneLiner: A horn-nosed theropod predator of the Late Jurassic.

txn:38607.description: Albertosaurus was a large tyrannosaurid predator of northwestern North America, with short arms, two-fingered hands and a massive head full of sharp teeth. Smaller than its famous relative Tyrannosaurus, it may still have been the apex predator of its ecosystem.

notableFacts.text: Had a strong sense of smell, powerful binocular vision and a bone-crushing bite.
A bonebed of many individuals hints it may have lived in groups.

txn:38607.oneLiner: A tyrannosaurid apex predator of latest-Cretaceous Alberta.

txn:38608.description: Daspletosaurus was a large bipedal tyrannosaurid from Late Cretaceous Laramidia (western North America), closely related to the later, larger Tyrannosaurus. Several species are known from Alberta and Montana.

notableFacts.text: One of the closest known relatives of Tyrannosaurus.
More robustly built than the contemporary Gorgosaurus.

txn:38608.oneLiner: A robust tyrannosaurid predator of Laramidia.

txn:38613.description: Tyrannosaurus was a large bipedal carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail and short but powerful two-clawed forelimbs. It ranged across western North America — then the island continent of Laramidia — at the very end of the Cretaceous, as the apex predator of its environment. Known from several nearly complete skeletons, it is one of the best-represented of all theropods.
txn:38613.nameMeaning: "Tyrant lizard"; the species name rex means 'king' in Latin

notableFacts.text: Its estimated bite force is the largest of any known land animal.
Ranged more widely than any other tyrannosaurid.
Soft tissue and proteins have been reported from at least one specimen.
Most likely both an apex predator and a scavenger.

txn:38613.oneLiner: A giant bipedal carnivorous theropod, among the largest land predators known.

txn:38642.description: Massospondylus was an early sauropodomorph from the Early Jurassic of southern Africa and one of the best-known of its group. Described by Richard Owen in 1854, it was among the first dinosaurs ever named. It is known from abundant specimens, including embryos preserved in eggs.

notableFacts.text: One of the first dinosaurs ever named (Owen, 1854).
Known from abundant specimens, including embryos inside eggs.
Owen named it 'longer vertebra' from bones he thought were from the tail — now known to be from the neck.

txn:38642.oneLiner: An Early Jurassic sauropodomorph, one of the first dinosaurs named.

txn:38644.description: Plateosaurus was an early sauropodomorph ('prosauropod') herbivore of Late Triassic Europe, known from abundant, well-preserved skeletons. It was one of the first dinosaurs to become well understood, and the fifth valid dinosaur genus ever named.

notableFacts.text: Known from abundant, well-preserved skeletons across central Europe.
The fifth still-valid dinosaur genus ever named.

txn:38644.oneLiner: A common Late Triassic 'prosauropod' of Europe.

txn:38665.description: Apatosaurus was a large, robustly built diplodocid sauropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America. It had a long neck, a whip-like tail held above the ground, and stockier, heavier bones than its relative Diplodocus. It was a browser that likely held its head elevated.

notableFacts.text: Stockier and more robustly built than its relative Diplodocus.
Its whip-like tail may have been cracked to make loud sounds.
Averaged 21–23 m; some individuals may have exceeded 30 m.

txn:38665.oneLiner: A massive, robust diplodocid sauropod of the Morrison Formation.

txn:38666.description: Barosaurus was an enormous diplodocid sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, closely related to Diplodocus, about 25–27 m long with a very long neck and whip-like tail.

notableFacts.text: Had an exceptionally long neck; a rearing mount towers in the American Museum of Natural History.
A close relative of Diplodocus.

txn:38666.oneLiner: A giant, long-necked diplodocid of the Morrison Formation.

txn:38669.description: Diplodocus was a very large, long-necked, quadrupedal sauropod with a long, whip-like tail and a largely horizontal posture. D. carnegii is one of the longest dinosaurs known from a complete skeleton, at 24–26 m. It lived in the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of western North America, where its great size may have deterred predators like Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus.

discovery.who: S. W. Williston (found); named by O. C. Marsh, 1878

txn:38669.nameMeaning: "Double beam", for the double-beamed chevron bones under its tail

notableFacts.text: One of the longest dinosaurs known from a complete skeleton (24–26 m).
Named "double beam" after the double-beamed chevron bones under its whip-like tail.
No skull can be confidently assigned to Diplodocus itself.

txn:38669.oneLiner: An enormous long-necked, whip-tailed diplodocid sauropod.

txn:38670.description: Mamenchisaurus was a sauropod of Jurassic China famous for its extraordinarily long neck — nearly half its total body length. Species ranged from roughly 15 to 26 m long, possibly up to 35 m.

notableFacts.text: Its neck made up nearly half its total body length — among the longest of any animal.
First found in 1952 at a Chinese highway construction site.

txn:38670.oneLiner: A Chinese sauropod with an extraordinarily long neck.

txn:38677.description: Brachiosaurus was a large sauropod with a disproportionately long neck, small skull, and — unusually — longer forelimbs than hindlimbs, giving it a steeply inclined trunk and a proportionally short tail. It lived in the Late Jurassic of North America and was a high browser, cropping vegetation up to about 9 m off the ground. Unlike other sauropods, it was unsuited to rearing on its hindlimbs.

discovery.where: Colorado River valley, western Colorado, USA

txn:38677.nameMeaning: "Arm lizard", for its proportionately long forelimbs

notableFacts.text: Unusually for a sauropod, its forelimbs were longer than its hindlimbs.
A high browser, cropping vegetation as high as ~9 m off the ground.
Most popular depictions are actually based on the African relative Giraffatitan.

txn:38677.oneLiner: A towering long-necked sauropod with longer arms than legs.

txn:38693.description: Saltasaurus was a small, stocky titanosaurian sauropod of Late Cretaceous Argentina with a short neck and stubby limbs. It was the first sauropod known to bear bony armour — small plates (osteoderms) embedded in its skin.

notableFacts.text: The first sauropod known to have bony armour plates in its skin.
Small and stocky, with a short neck and stubby limbs.

txn:38693.oneLiner: An armoured titanosaur sauropod of Late Cretaceous Argentina.

txn:38697.description: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod with a proportionally short neck, a large, strongly built skull and powerful jaws bearing spoon-shaped teeth. The most common dinosaur of the Morrison Formation of western North America and one of the best-understood sauropods, it is known from over 530 specimens. It was probably a selective browser feeding 2–5 m off the ground.
txn:38697.nameMeaning: "Chambered lizard", for the hollow chambers in its vertebrae

notableFacts.text: The most common dinosaur of the Morrison Formation.
Powerful jaws and spoon-shaped teeth suited it to tough plants.
One specimen may have reached about 40 years old — among the oldest ages reported for a dinosaur.

txn:38697.oneLiner: The most common sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation.

txn:38731.description: Dryosaurus was a small iguanodont ornithopod of the Late Jurassic of the western United States, an agile bipedal herbivore up to about 3 m long. It had a horny beak and cheek teeth for processing plants.

notableFacts.text: A small, fast-running bipedal herbivore.
Cropped plants with a horny beak and cheek teeth.

txn:38731.oneLiner: A small, fast, bipedal ornithopod of the Late Jurassic.

txn:38736.description: Hypsilophodon was a small, agile, bipedal herbivore of the Early Cretaceous of England, 1.5–2 m long, with a beaked, pointed head. Abundant finds on the Isle of Wight give a clear picture of its build.

notableFacts.text: A small, fleet-footed bipedal herbivore.
Older ideas that it was tree-climbing and armoured have since been disproven.

txn:38736.oneLiner: A small, agile herbivore famous from the Isle of Wight.

txn:38741.description: Tenontosaurus was a medium-sized iguanodontian ornithopod with an unusually long, broad tail stiffened by a network of bony tendons. It lived in Early Cretaceous western North America and is often found associated with the predator Deinonychus.
txn:38741.nameMeaning: "Sinew lizard", for its tendon-stiffened back and tail

notableFacts.text: Its long tail and back were stiffened by a network of bony tendons.
Frequently found alongside the predator Deinonychus.

txn:38741.oneLiner: A medium-sized ornithopod with an unusually long, stiffened tail.

txn:38742.description: Thescelosaurus was a small, heavily built ornithischian herbivore of Late Cretaceous western North America, 3–4 m long, with a long low snout ending in a beak and a stiffened tail. It was among the last non-avian dinosaurs.

notableFacts.text: One of the last non-avian dinosaurs before the extinction.
Its long tail was stiffened by rod-like ossified tendons.

txn:38742.oneLiner: A sturdy small ornithischian of the very end of the Cretaceous.

txn:38748.description: Camptosaurus was a plant-eating, beaked ornithopod of the Late Jurassic of western North America, a heavier-bodied relative of Iguanodon. It could walk on two legs or four.

notableFacts.text: An early, sturdy relative of Iguanodon.
Could move on two legs or four.

txn:38748.oneLiner: A sturdy, beaked ornithopod of the Late Jurassic.

txn:38749.description: Iguanodon was a large, bulky herbivore up to 9–11 m long from the Early Cretaceous of Europe, distinguished by large thumb spikes — possibly for defence — and long prehensile fifth fingers for foraging. One of the first dinosaurs ever named, it was among the three genera originally used to define Dinosauria.

notableFacts.text: Had large thumb spikes, possibly used for defence.
The second dinosaur ever formally named, and one of three used to define Dinosauria.
Superb complete skeletons were found in a Belgian coal mine in 1878.

txn:38749.oneLiner: A large, bulky iguanodontian herbivore with a spiked thumb.

txn:38751.description: Ouranosaurus was a basal hadrosauriform ornithopod herbivore of Early Cretaceous Niger and Cameroon, 7–8.3 m long. It bore tall spines along its back that may have supported a sail or a fatty hump.

notableFacts.text: Bore tall back spines that may have supported a sail or a hump.
An early relative of the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

txn:38751.oneLiner: A sail-backed iguanodontian of Cretaceous Africa.

txn:38760.description: Corythosaurus was a lambeosaurine 'duck-billed' hadrosaur about 8–9 m long, famous for its tall, hollow, helmet-like head crest. The crest most likely amplified calls, working like a resonating trombone. It is known from many complete specimens, some with preserved skin.

notableFacts.text: Its hollow crest likely resonated to produce calls, like a trombone.
Some specimens preserve impressions of its polygonal scales.

txn:38760.oneLiner: A crested duck-billed hadrosaur of Late Cretaceous Alberta.

txn:38761.description: Edmontosaurus was one of the largest hadrosaurids (duck-billed dinosaurs), reaching about 12 m long, with exceptional individuals near 15 m. It lived in Late Cretaceous western North America alongside Triceratops and Tyrannosaurus and was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs. Several specimens preserve extensive skin impressions and possible gut contents.

notableFacts.text: One of the largest hadrosaurs — up to ~12 m, exceptional individuals ~15 m.
Known from specimens with extensive skin impressions and possible gut contents.
One of the last non-avian dinosaurs, living alongside T. rex and Triceratops.

txn:38761.oneLiner: A giant duck-billed hadrosaur, among the last non-avian dinosaurs.

txn:38763.description: Lambeosaurus was a lambeosaurine 'duck-billed' hadrosaur of Late Cretaceous western North America, with a distinctive hollow head crest. It is the namesake of the lambeosaurine hadrosaurs.

notableFacts.text: Named for the hollow, often hatchet-shaped head crest characteristic of its group.
Named to honour paleontologist Lawrence Lambe.

txn:38763.oneLiner: A hollow-crested duck-billed hadrosaur of western North America.

txn:38765.description: Maiasaura was a large duck-billed hadrosaur of Late Cretaceous Montana, discovered at a nesting site during the 'dinosaur renaissance'. Evidence that it fed its young in the nest gave the first proof of parental and social behaviour in dinosaurs — hence 'good mother lizard'.

notableFacts.text: Its nesting colonies gave the first evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.
'Good mother lizard' — a rare feminine dinosaur name.

txn:38765.oneLiner: A hadrosaur that gave the first evidence of dinosaur parental care.

txn:38766.description: Parasaurolophus was a large hadrosaurid ('duck-billed' dinosaur) from the Late Cretaceous of western North America, over 9 m long. It is known for its long, curved, tube-like cranial crest, likely used for visual display and to produce resonating calls. It could move on two legs or four.

notableFacts.text: Its long, curved, hollow crest may have resonated like a trumpet.
The crest likely served for species and sex recognition and acoustic signalling.

txn:38766.oneLiner: A duck-billed hadrosaur famous for its long, curved head crest.

txn:38768.description: Saurolophus was a large duck-billed hadrosaur of the Late Cretaceous, distinguished by a spike-like crest projecting up and back from its skull. Unusually, it is known from both North America and Asia.

notableFacts.text: Bore a solid spike-like crest projecting up and back from the skull.
One of the few dinosaur genera known from two continents.

txn:38768.oneLiner: A spike-crested hadrosaur known from two continents.

txn:38786.description: Pachycephalosaurus was a bipedal ornithischian herbivore from the very end of the Cretaceous in western North America, and the largest known pachycephalosaur at about 4.5 m long. It is famous for its extremely thick, domed skull roof — up to 22 cm thick — which may have been used for head-butting displays or combat.

notableFacts.text: Its skull roof was up to 22 cm thick — the thickest of any known dinosaur.
The dome may have been used for head-butting, like bighorn sheep.
The genera Stygimoloch and Dracorex may just be its growth stages.

txn:38786.oneLiner: A bipedal herbivore with an extremely thick, domed skull.

txn:38787.description: Stegoceras was a small bipedal pachycephalosaur ('dome-headed' dinosaur) of Late Cretaceous North America, 2–2.5 m long, with a thick, broad dome on top of its skull. It is one of the better-known pachycephalosaurs.

notableFacts.text: Had a thick bony dome on its skull, likely used in display or combat.
One of the best-known dome-headed dinosaurs.

txn:38811.description: Kentrosaurus was a stegosaur of the Late Jurassic of Tanzania, a close relative of Stegosaurus, with plates on its neck and shoulders giving way to paired spikes along its back and tail. Hundreds of its bones were unearthed by German expeditions to Tendaguru.

notableFacts.text: Wore plates over the neck and shoulders and paired spikes along the back and tail.
A close African relative of the North American Stegosaurus.

txn:38811.oneLiner: An African stegosaur bristling with plates and spikes.

txn:38814.description: Stegosaurus was a large, heavily built herbivorous quadruped with a rounded back, short forelimbs, a small head, and distinctive kite-shaped upright plates along its back with spikes on its tail. It lived in the Late Jurassic of the western United States and Portugal, alongside Apatosaurus, Diplodocus and Allosaurus. Its tail spikes were most likely defensive, while its plates were probably used for display and thermoregulation.

notableFacts.text: Bore distinctive kite-shaped back plates, likely used for display and thermoregulation.
Its spiked tail was most likely used to defend against predators like Allosaurus.
Had a relatively low brain-to-body mass ratio and a small head.

txn:38814.oneLiner: A plated, spike-tailed herbivorous armoured dinosaur.

txn:38823.description: Nodosaurus was a nodosaurid ankylosaur — an armoured herbivore without a tail club — from the Late Cretaceous of Wyoming. It was one of the first armoured dinosaurs described from North America.

notableFacts.text: Its back was covered in bands of bony armour, but it lacked a tail club.
One of the first armoured dinosaurs named from North America, during the Bone Wars.

txn:38823.oneLiner: An armoured nodosaur from the Cretaceous of Wyoming.

txn:38827.description: Sauropelta was a nodosaurid — an armoured dinosaur without a tail club — of Early Cretaceous North America, about 5–6 m long. It carried extensive bony armour and large spines projecting from its neck, and had an unusually long tail.

notableFacts.text: Bore large defensive spines projecting from its neck.
Its long tail made up about half its body length — but had no club.

txn:38827.oneLiner: An Early Cretaceous nodosaur with long neck spines.

txn:38837.description: Ankylosaurus was a heavily armoured dinosaur from the very end of the Cretaceous in western North America, and the largest known ankylosaurid at 6–8 m long. Its broad, low body was covered in bony plates (osteoderms), and its tail ended in a large bony club. It was among the last non-avian dinosaurs.

notableFacts.text: Its tail ended in a large bony club, likely used in defence.
Covered in bony plates (osteoderms), even over the eyelids.
'Fused lizard' — many of its bones were fused together for strength.

txn:38837.oneLiner: The archetypal armoured dinosaur, with a bony tail club.

txn:38838.description: Euoplocephalus was a large ankylosaurid of Late Cretaceous Canada, 5.3 m long and about 2 tonnes, with a low, flat, wide body covered in bony armour — even over the eyelids — and a heavy bony tail club. It is one of the best-known armoured dinosaurs.

notableFacts.text: Had a heavy bony club on the end of its tail.
Armoured even over the eyelids.

txn:38844.description: Psittacosaurus was a small early ceratopsian from the Early Cretaceous of Asia — a biped with a high skull and a robust parrot-like beak. It is the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus and one of the most completely known, from hundreds of individuals. One specimen preserves long bristle-like filaments on the tail.

notableFacts.text: The most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus — up to 13 species.
Had a robust parrot-like beak.
One specimen preserves long bristle-like filaments on the tail.
One of the most completely known dinosaurs — hundreds of individuals found.

txn:38844.oneLiner: A small, early bipedal ceratopsian with a parrot-like beak.

txn:38848.description: Protoceratops was a small ceratopsian from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, 2–2.5 m long, with a proportionally large skull, a neck frill and a prominent parrot-like beak — but no true horns. The frill was likely used for display, combat and muscle attachment. It is extremely well known from the Mongolian Gobi.

notableFacts.text: Had a bony neck frill and parrot-like beak, but no true horns.
Its Gobi nests were once wrongly blamed on Oviraptor, thought to be raiding them.
One of the best-known dinosaurs, from hatchling to adult.

txn:38848.oneLiner: A small, frilled ceratopsian of the Late Cretaceous Gobi Desert.

txn:38854.description: Centrosaurus was a centrosaurine horned dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada, with a single nasal horn and small hornlets along the margin of its frill. It is known from vast bonebeds containing thousands of individuals — possibly herds that drowned crossing flooded rivers.
txn:38854.nameMeaning: "Pointed lizard", for the hornlets on its frill

notableFacts.text: Known from vast bonebeds with thousands of individuals — likely mass-drowned herds.
Named for the small hornlets along the margin of its frill.

txn:38854.oneLiner: A horned ceratopsian known from immense Alberta bonebeds.

txn:38855.description: Chasmosaurus was a mid-sized chasmosaurine horned dinosaur of Late Cretaceous Alberta, 4.3–4.8 m long, named for the large openings (fenestrae) in its neck frill. Many specimens come from Dinosaur Provincial Park.
txn:38855.nameMeaning: "Opening lizard", for the openings in its frill

notableFacts.text: Its large neck frill was lightened by big openings (fenestrae).

txn:38855.oneLiner: A ceratopsian with a large, fenestrated neck frill.

txn:38858.description: Pachyrhinosaurus was a centrosaurine horned dinosaur of Late Cretaceous North America (Alberta to Alaska), notable for a thick, flat bony boss over its nose and eyes instead of horns. It is known from over a dozen skulls and rich bonebeds.

notableFacts.text: Had a massive bony boss over the nose instead of a horn.
One species lived as far north as Arctic Alaska.

txn:38858.oneLiner: A horned ceratopsian with a massive bony nose boss.

txn:38860.description: Styracosaurus was a large horned dinosaur of Late Cretaceous North America, bearing four to six long spikes on its neck frill and a single long nose horn. A bulky quadrupedal herbivore, it sliced plants with shearing cheek-teeth and may have lived in herds.

notableFacts.text: Bore four to six long spikes on its neck frill plus a long nose horn.
Its nose horn may have reached 60 cm long.

txn:38860.oneLiner: A horned ceratopsian with a spectacular spiked frill.

txn:38861.description: Torosaurus was a chasmosaurine ceratopsian of the very end of the Cretaceous, 7.5–9 m long, possessing an enormous elongated frill with large openings — giving it one of the largest skulls of any known land animal (up to 2.77 m). Some researchers argue it is simply a fully mature Triceratops.
txn:38861.nameMeaning: "Perforated lizard", for the openings in its frill

notableFacts.text: Its frilled skull (up to 2.77 m) is among the largest of any land animal.
Debated to be the mature adult form of Triceratops.

txn:38861.oneLiner: A ceratopsian bearing one of the largest skulls of any land animal.

txn:38862.description: Triceratops was a large four-legged herbivore bearing a bony frill and three facial horns, showing convergent evolution with rhinoceroses. It lived on Laramidia (western North America) at the very end of the Cretaceous and shared its landscape with — and was most likely preyed on by — Tyrannosaurus. The best-known ceratopsian, it is documented from many specimens spanning hatchling to adult.

notableFacts.text: Bore three facial horns and a large bony frill, likely used in display and species recognition.
Some research argues Torosaurus is just the mature form of Triceratops — still disputed.
Shared its world with Tyrannosaurus and was most likely preyed upon by it.

txn:38862.oneLiner: A large horned, frilled herbivorous ceratopsian.

txn:39240.description: Archaeopteryx is a famous bird-like dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of southern Germany, long regarded as the earliest known bird. About the size of a magpie (up to ~50 cm long), it combined feathers and wings with reptilian features — toothed jaws, clawed fingers and a long bony tail — a classic transitional fossil between non-avian dinosaurs and birds.

notableFacts.text: A classic transitional fossil between non-avian dinosaurs and birds.
Its preserved feathers were among the first evidence linking birds to dinosaurs.
Combined bird-like feathers and wings with dinosaur teeth, clawed fingers and a bony tail.

txn:39240.oneLiner: The famous feathered 'first bird', a transitional Jurassic dinosaur.

txn:52983.description: Brontosaurus was a large diplodocid sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, the archetypal 'long-necked dinosaur' in popular culture. Long treated as a synonym of Apatosaurus, a 2015 study restored it as a distinct genus.

notableFacts.text: The archetypal 'long-necked' dinosaur of popular culture.
Long sunk into Apatosaurus, it was restored as a separate genus in 2015.

txn:52983.oneLiner: The archetypal long-necked sauropod of the Morrison Formation.

txn:53014.description: Gryposaurus was a duck-billed hadrosaur of Late Cretaceous North America, easily recognised by its narrow, arching 'Roman nose' nasal hump. It is known from many skulls, skeletons and even skin impressions showing pyramidal scales along the back.

notableFacts.text: Named for its distinctive narrow, arched 'Roman nose' nasal hump.
Skin impressions show pyramidal scales along its back.

txn:53014.oneLiner: A duck-billed hadrosaur with a distinctive arched nose.

txn:53193.description: Gorgosaurus was a large bipedal tyrannosaurid predator of western North America, 8–9 m long, with dozens of sharp teeth and small two-fingered arms. It was a close relative of Albertosaurus and a more distant cousin of Tyrannosaurus.

notableFacts.text: A close relative of Albertosaurus, and among the best-known tyrannosaurids.
Like other tyrannosaurids, it had tiny two-fingered forelimbs.

txn:53193.oneLiner: A large tyrannosaurid predator of Late Cretaceous Alberta.

txn:53960.description: Amargasaurus was a small dicraeosaurid sauropod of Early Cretaceous Argentina, 9–13 m long, known from a nearly complete skeleton. It is unique for two parallel rows of tall spines running down its neck and back — taller than in any other sauropod.

notableFacts.text: Bore two parallel rows of tall neck spines, possibly supporting sails or a horn sheath.
Known from a nearly complete skeleton — rare for a sauropod.

txn:53960.oneLiner: A small sauropod sporting a double row of tall neck spines.

txn:54533.description: Carnotaurus was a lightly built bipedal predator from the Late Cretaceous of Argentina, 7.5–8 m long. It is unique among carnivorous dinosaurs in having two thick horns above its eyes, on a deep skull and muscular neck. It had extremely small, vestigial forelimbs and long, slender legs, and its skin is preserved as a mosaic of small scales.
txn:54533.nameMeaning: "Meat-eating bull", for its bull-like brow horns

notableFacts.text: The only carnivorous dinosaur with two thick brow horns.
Had extremely small, vestigial forelimbs — even shorter than T. rex's.
Known from extensive skin impressions of small, non-overlapping scales.

txn:54533.oneLiner: A horned, tiny-armed abelisaurid predator of Cretaceous South America.

txn:54540.description: Giganotosaurus was a giant carcharodontosaurid theropod of Late Cretaceous Argentina and one of the largest known land carnivores, roughly 12–13 m long. Its holotype is about 70% complete, making it one of the better-known giant predators of the Southern Hemisphere.

notableFacts.text: Among the largest known land carnivores — rivalling or exceeding T. rex in length.
Its skull alone measured over 1.5 m long.

txn:54540.oneLiner: One of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs, from Patagonia.

txn:54548.description: Sinosauropteryx was a small coelurosaurian theropod of Early Cretaceous China with a long tail and short arms, about 1 m long. Described in 1996, it was the first dinosaur outside the bird lineage found with feathers — simple filaments — and preserved pigment shows it had a countershaded body and a banded tail.

notableFacts.text: The first non-avian dinosaur found with evidence of feathers.
Preserved pigment reveals a countershaded body and a banded 'raccoon' tail.

txn:54548.oneLiner: The first non-bird dinosaur found with feathers — and known colours.

txn:54557.description: Utahraptor was the largest known dromaeosaurid ('raptor'), a heavily built, ground-dwelling carnivore of Early Cretaceous Utah, about 6–7 m long and ~500 kg. Its feet bore an enlarged sickle-shaped killing claw.

notableFacts.text: The largest known member of the dromaeosaurid ('raptor') family.
Bore a large sickle-shaped killing claw on each foot.

txn:54557.oneLiner: The largest known raptor, a heavy Early Cretaceous dromaeosaur.

txn:56405.description: Hypacrosaurus was a lambeosaurine 'duck-billed' hadrosaur of Late Cretaceous Alberta and Montana, similar to Corythosaurus but with a lower rounded crest. It is well known from nests, eggs and hatchlings — the latest good hollow-crested hadrosaur in North America.

notableFacts.text: Known from nests, eggs and hatchlings, illuminating hadrosaur growth.
Had a tall, hollow, rounded head crest.

txn:56405.oneLiner: A hollow-crested hadrosaur known from nests and hatchlings.

txn:57366.description: Nigersaurus was a small rebbachisaurid sauropod of mid-Cretaceous Niger, about 9 m long with a short neck and a bizarre, highly specialised skull. Its wide, straight-edged muzzle held more than 500 teeth, replaced roughly every two weeks, for cropping ground-level plants.

notableFacts.text: Its wide muzzle held over 500 teeth, replaced about every 14 days.
Had an extremely lightweight, specialised skull for ground-level grazing.

txn:57366.oneLiner: A wide-mouthed sauropod with over 500 teeth.

txn:57453.description: Eoraptor was a small, lightly built early sauropodomorph of the Late Triassic of Argentina and one of the earliest known dinosaurs. Its varied tooth shapes suggest it was omnivorous.

notableFacts.text: One of the earliest known dinosaurs.
Its mix of tooth shapes points to an omnivorous diet.

txn:57453.oneLiner: A tiny, early omnivorous dinosaur near the dawn of the group.

txn:58891.description: Baryonyx was a spinosaurid theropod from the Early Cretaceous of England, 7.5–10 m long, with a long, low, narrow crocodile-like snout and a very large claw on each first finger. Its numerous conical teeth and gharial-like jaws suited a fish-eating (and partly predatory) diet.
txn:58891.nameMeaning: "Heavy claw", for its large thumb claw

notableFacts.text: Named for the very large claw on each hand.
Its long, narrow, crocodile-like snout suited catching fish.
One of the most complete theropod skeletons found in the UK.

txn:58891.oneLiner: A fish-eating spinosaur with a crocodile-like snout and huge claw.

txn:64371.description: Cryolophosaurus was a large theropod of the Early Jurassic of Antarctica, 6–7 m long, with a distinctive crest running across the top of its skull. It was the first carnivorous dinosaur discovered on the continent and the first Antarctic dinosaur to be formally named.

notableFacts.text: The first carnivorous dinosaur discovered in Antarctica.
Had an unusual crest running side-to-side across its skull.

txn:64371.oneLiner: The first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica.

txn:66645.description: Argentinosaurus was a giant titanosaurian sauropod of Late Cretaceous Argentina and one of the largest land animals ever, estimated at 30–35 m long and 65–80 tonnes — though it is known only from fragmentary remains.

notableFacts.text: Among the largest land animals ever to have lived.
Its size is estimated from only a few giant vertebrae and limb bones.

txn:66645.oneLiner: A titanosaur among the largest land animals of all time.

txn:68238.description: Microraptor was a small four-winged dromaeosaurid from Early Cretaceous China, known from many superb feathered fossils. Long flight feathers on both its arms and legs formed four aerodynamic surfaces, and it may have glided between trees.

notableFacts.text: Had flight feathers on both arms and legs — a 'four-winged' dinosaur.
May have glided between trees; its fossils inform the origin of bird flight.
Preserved melanosomes suggest an iridescent black plumage.

txn:68238.oneLiner: A tiny, four-winged, gliding feathered dinosaur.
